report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: We derive an exact, sharp lower bound for Hartigan's dip on lattice-supported questionnaire scores and characterise two further identification limits on latent-distribution shape.
If 𝑞 (2) is the mass of the second-largest score atom, then 𝐷 ≥ 𝑞 (2) /2.

Across nine public collections (2.48 million records; 48 score series), all 48 reject under the diptest calibration at a common 𝑛 = 12 000; 28 lie on the atom floor to four decimals, 34 are within one per cent, and the floor alone crosses the rejection threshold for all 48, with median sample-size crossing 𝑛 * = 539.
After within-cell perturbation removes the lattice, 47 series reject in none of 100 replications and one in all.

Latent modality is also not invariant under the strictly increasing reparametrisations left free by a nonparametric item-response model; a five-standard-deviation mixture can be transformed to pass the dip test without changing ranks.
Finally, fixing a metric does not identify the latent law: under a continuous finite item-response design, a relative-interior observable admits both atomic and atomless mixing distributions.
Fisherinformation arc length supplies an item-anchored coordinate, but finite-design identified uncertainty remains.
An attribute is measured by a questionnaire; the responses are added; the total is examined for structure.
Two modes separated by a valley are reported as evidence of two kinds of respondent, one mode as evidence of a continuum.

The question is pursued continually: on autistic traits (Frazier et al., 2023), on personality types (Gerlach et al., 2018), and across the psychopathology literature reviewed by Haslam et al. (2012 Haslam et al. ( , 2020)).

text.text: Those studies use a range of procedures, most of which lie outside the scope of the results below.

text.text: We show that this inference is blocked by three distinct limits: the support of the observed score, the freedom to reparametrise the latent coordinate, and the non-singleton identified set left by a finite item design.
None is repaired by collecting more respondents.

Equivalently, they are three identification requirements for a defensible modality claim: the observable must not make the test reject mechanically, the latent metric must make shape well defined, and the measurement design must identify the feature being interpreted.

One line of research on latent kinds has used tests of distributional shape, whereas psychometric identification theory asks which properties of a latent variable are determined by an item response model.

The two literatures meet at the question considered here: before a mode, a gap or a class is interpreted substantively, both the response format of the observable and the identifying conventions of the latent scale have to be specified.

Nonparametric modality inference (Hartigan & Hartigan, 1985; Müller & Sawitzki, 1991; Silverman, 1981) is a theory about samples from distributions the analyst observes directly; the identification results (Lord, 1975; Ramsay, 1996; Rossi et al., 2002; Allman et al., 2009) concern what a finite item set determines about a variable nobody observes.

text.text: Neither supplies the object in between.
The paper's distinctive contribution is concentrated in the first link and in what the links establish together.

Proposition 1 gives an exact, sharp lower bound for the dip on an arbitrary atomic distribution, identifies the second-largest atom as the binding quantity, and yields a sample-size crossing diagnostic that can be read directly from score counts.

In the empirical corpus the bound is not a small correction: 28 of 48 score series sit on it to four decimals, 34 lie within one per cent, and at the common sample size the floor alone crosses the test calibration for every series.
The remaining results show why moving from the total to an estimated latent density does not, by itself, rescue the intended inference.

Its functional is central-window mass, not modality, a gap or atomicity; no bounding relation between that functional and modality is asserted.
It also uses a total-score observable, which coarsens the full response pattern, stylised item parameters, and a discretised latent support.

Within those restrictions, the calculation shows that partial identification of a local distributional feature can remain substantial at questionnaire-sized finite designs even when the manifest score distribution is known exactly.
In small designs where both observables can be computed, retaining only the total widens the identified range by 15-37 per cent.
Across the stylised design sequence the range contracts as items are added, but at each fixed finite 𝐽 respondent sample size does not enter the fibre.
The detailed levels and design screen belong to the numerical illustration rather than to the theorem and are reported in Online Resource 1, Appendix E.

The three limits above can be read positively as identification requirements: they state what an analysis must supply before a claim about latent modality has a well-defined target and support in the observable data.

Modality of a latent density is meaningful only relative to a stated metric.

Theorem 3 is not a caution about estimation error: the class of models observationally equivalent to any given one contains members whose latent density has any modality one specifies, with every respondent in the same rank position.
A reported bimodality is a joint statement about the population and about a coordinate the analyst chose, usually by adopting a parametric link without comment.
An item-anchored coordinate can make shape well defined, but does not restore identification.

Once the item-response functions are specified, an item-anchored coordinate (Fisher-information arc length here, surprisal-based alternatives elsewhere (Wallmark & Wiberg, 2026)) is invariant to smooth increasing reparametrisation of the latent coordinate; the cost is that the resulting statement is a property of the pair (attribute, item set) rather than an instrument-free population shape.

text.text: Fixing it does not make the latent distribution identified.

A researcher may assume a finite latent-class model and, under suitable rank/category conditions, identify its mixing proportions and class-specific response probabilities; what the unrestricted data will not do, at a relative-interior observable covered by Proposition 5, is adjudicate the finite-class assumption.
A finite instrument identifies only a set of latent distributions.

This is where the practical message departs from the usual one: At fixed finite design and manifest distribution, identified uncertainty about a latent-distribution feature need not vanish as the respondent sample grows.
Reducing it requires a more informative observable design or additional model restrictions, not merely more respondents.

Increasing the sample from 12 000 to 1.02 million estimates the observable distribution more precisely, but does not by itself shrink the fibre or the identified range; what distinguishes the designs in Online Resource 1, Appendix E is their length and response format.
Therefore a claim about latent classes requires assumptions, design information and sensitivity analysis, not a large sample and a shape test.
For a dip analysis of a questionnaire score, a minimum report is the lattice floor 𝑞 (2) /2, the ratio 𝐷 𝑛 /{ 𝑞 (2) /2}, and whether the floor alone forces rejection under the stated calibration.

A claim about latent shape additionally has to state the response model and latent metric that make shape meaningful, and distinguish assumptions that fix the scale from assumptions or design information that identify the mixing law.

Three developments would settle more: sharp bounds for identified ranges of modality-relevant functionals; a cross-instrument study using common respondents and a flexible latent-density model to assess the practical size of item-relative metric effects; and an analysis of what the covariance-based taxometric procedures estimate under (5).
Applying Hartigan's dip test directly to a questionnaire total does not establish whether a latent attribute is categorical or dimensional.
First, the total is lattice-supported, so the dip has an atom-induced floor that can itself cross the rejection threshold as the sample grows.
Second, latent modality is coordinatedependent under the monotone reparametrisations left free by a nonparametric item-response model.

Third, fixing a coordinate does not identify an unrestricted mixing law at finite 𝐽: every relative-interior observable covered by the continuous-curve result is compatible with both atomic and atomless latent laws.

An item-anchored coordinate can make a shape statement well defined, but identified uncertainty then remains a property of the finite design, observable and functional, not something respondent sample size alone removes.

B.1 Sources Open-Source Psychometrics Project.

Six collections (NPAS, DASS, EQSQ, IPIP-FFM, IPIP-16PF, HEXACO) come from this project (Open-Source Psychometrics Project, 2019), which distributes raw responses to online assessments, several based on public-domain item sets, with a codebook for each.
Respondents were volunteers who reached the site and elected to complete a test in exchange for personalised feedback; those in the distributed files consented to research use.
The samples are convenience samples not selected by diagnostic class and are predominantly English-speaking.

This does not affect the theorems, which concern what an instrument of given size can resolve; it does affect the observed atom masses and their scaling with scale length, and therefore the empirical figures in the results section of the main text, which should be read as descriptions of these collections rather than of any defined population.

The instruments are the Nerdy Personality Attributes Scale (26 items, collected December 2015 to December 2018); the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995 , 42 items, collected 2017 to 2019); the Systemising Quotient (Baron-Cohen et al., 2003, 60 items; see below on the composition of this file); the IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers (Goldberg, 1992 (Goldberg, , 50 items, collected 2016 (Goldberg, to 2018)); a set of 163 public-domain IPIP items keyed to constructs resembling Cattell's sixteen factors, which is not the proprietary 16PF and is labelled IPIP-16PF throughout; and the HEXACO-240 (Lee & Ashton, 2004, 240 items).

Because that perturbation is random, the test applied after it is a random test and a single application reports one realisation; it was therefore repeated 100 times per scale and the distribution of the outcome recorded, a scale being counted as rejecting only if it rejects in a majority of its perturbations.

Two properties of the uncorrected operation were also recorded: the statistic recomputed at a common sample size across collections, separating it from the 𝑛 at which it happens to be available; and one distribution resampled at increasing 𝑛, exhibiting the dependence of the rejection rate on sample size at constant shape.

Where a scale continued to reject, the modal interval was inspected and the perturbed test repeated, over the same 100 replications, on respondents more than one response category from either boundary.
The association between 𝑞 (2) and the number of items summed was summarised by a descriptive log-log regression across scales.

For each score series the atom-bound crossing point was found numerically as the smallest 𝑛 for which √ 𝑛 𝑞 (2) /2 exceeds the 0.05 critical value, using the same interpolation of the diptest package's qDiptab table as dip.test.

The reparametrisation families are 𝑔 𝑠 (𝑧) = Φ(𝑧/𝑠), with 𝑔 ′ 𝑠 = 𝜑(𝑧/𝑠)/𝑠 maximal at 𝑧 = 0, and ℎ 𝑎 (𝑧) = sinh(𝑎𝑧)/𝑎, with ℎ ′ 𝑎 = cosh(𝑎𝑧) minimal there; the two move the density in opposite directions and ℎ 𝑎 → id as 𝑎 → 0.

They are used for exposition and are not claimed to be the transformation implicit in any published analysis: they are members of the class left free by the observable map, and their sufficiency to reverse a conclusion is the point at issue.

The latent grid is coarsened as the design lengthens.
Adjacent columns of the observable map become nearly indistinguishable on a fine grid for a long instrument and the solver stalls; the behaviour at 𝐽 = 320 is described below.
Each of the three transitions of the resulting rule was audited by solving the same design on both adjacent grids, with the design chosen so that the two grids differ.
All three solved on both.

Ranges differed by between 2.8 and 4.8 per cent, and the deficit by between 0.18 and 0.51 percentage points, in the direction the discretisation argument predicts, the finer grid giving the larger range in every case.
Those figures measure local sensitivity to the grid transition; they do not bound the error relative to the continuous fibre.
The largest deficit change, 0.51 percentage points, is the tolerance carried to the design screen.
Small coefficients are dropped, and at long designs this matters.
The operative threshold is 10 -9 : coefficients below it are discarded whatever value is requested, and on the longest designs a large share of the matrix entries falls below it.

Raising the threshold by two orders of magnitude, to 10 -7 , leaves short designs almost unchanged and moves long ones appreciably: the relative change in the computed range is 0.03 per cent at 𝐽 = 10, 𝐾 = 5 and 0.20 per cent at 𝐽 = 26, 𝐾 = 5, but 8.3 per cent at 𝐽 = 60, 𝐾 = 5 and 4.6 per cent at 𝐽 = 40, 𝐾 = 7.
The larger figures exceed the grid sensitivity reported above.
The computation at long designs is therefore not insensitive to where the coefficient threshold sits, and the reported ranges carry that uncertainty in addition to the discretisation one.
The direction is not perfectly monotone: the higher threshold gives a slightly larger range at 𝐽 = 26, 𝐾 = 5 and smaller ranges in the other three audited designs.
We therefore treat the comparison as a sensitivity diagnostic rather than as a one-sided bound.
The audit of support truncation is a nested one, and it measures numerical uncertainty rather than a support effect.
The support is truncated at [-5, 5].

text.text: Truncation removes candidates from the feasible set, so a wider support cannot narrow the identified range, but only if the observable, the objective and the reference value are held fixed.

Recomputing the reference law on each support would change all three, the discretised normal being renormalised over a different interval, and the fibres would then not be nested; a wider support could return a narrower range for reasons that are not numerical error.
The reference law is therefore computed once on the working grid and embedded in the wider grids with zero weight outside it.

Because the grid spacing is held constant at 0.00417, each wider grid contains the working one exactly, so the observable, the objective vector and the reference value are identical across supports by construction; both the containment and the invariance of the observable are asserted at run time rather than assumed.
Under binary designs the range then increases monotonically with the support, from 0.38177 at half-width 5 to 0.38294 and 0.38334 at 6 and 7, as it must.
Across the four instrument-matched designs the largest increase on a wider support is 1.5 × 10 -4 and the largest decrease 5.8 × 10 -3 .
Because the feasible sets nest, a decrease cannot be a support effect, so that figure is a direct measurement of numerical error in the computed range.
It is of the same order as the grid sensitivity reported above, and is a third quantity the reported ranges carry.

No substantial expansion was observed on any wider support, so truncation at the working support does not appear to constrain the extremising law materially; the non-monotone decreases place the numerical uncertainty at roughly the order of the grid audit.
The audit uses the objective fixed in the parametric coordinate.

The arc-length objective is not audited: its interval is defined as a fraction of a total arc length that the support itself changes, so the two effects would not be separable without a further convention.
Designs at 𝐽 = 320 display non-monotone solver behaviour.
Solved on grids of 1201, 601 and 301 points, the finest and the coarsest return while the intermediate one does not, and the two values returned differ materially.
Solver success at these lengths is therefore not monotone in the grid resolution, and the values that are returned are strongly grid-dependent.
These designs are excluded from the design screen and from every fitted quantity, and are reported as a demonstration of that behaviour rather than as estimates.

The arc-length proposition identifies information arc length as a parametrisation fixed by the item set, whereas the computations above fix the interval in the coordinate of the assumed parametric family.

Both were therefore computed on the same fibre, differing only in the objective vector: the observable map, the reference law and the grid are identical, and the interval in the second case is the central twenty per cent of the design's total information arc length.

The information used to define that coordinate is the full item-response Fisher information even though the identified-range calculation deliberately coarsens the observable to the total score; the metric anchors the item-response curve and does not add pattern-level constraints to the score-only fibre.

text.text: Five restrictions deserve scrutiny, in addition to the three stated in the scope subsection of the main text.
First, conditional independence.
It is the standard assumption of the field and it is an assumption.

It is also the one under which the reparametrisation argument is cleanest: a violation introduces dependence among responses that is not absorbed by any transformation of 𝜃, and would in principle carry information about the metric.

Whether residual dependence is informative enough to restrict the reparametrisation group in practice is open, and would be a constructive route to fixing the metric that does not require a convention.
Secondly, monotonicity of the item response functions.
The invariance theorem uses it only to check that the transformed model remains in P; the observational equivalence in (i) holds without it.
Relaxing monotonicity therefore widens rather than narrows the indeterminacy.
Thirdly, the empirical work is confined to sum scores.

This is the literature's practice and is not an endorsement of it: the whole of the lattice section of the main text is an argument against the practice, and a reader who concludes that the response patterns should be modelled directly has taken the intended point.
The sum score is analysed because it is what the findings under examination were computed from.
Fourthly, the perturbation removing the lattice is a diagnostic and not an estimator.

It does not estimate the distribution of the underlying variable, and the near-unity 𝑝-values it returns should not be read as evidence of unimodality in any object other than the perturbed score.
Fifthly, the dip is one modality statistic among several, and only the dip is analysed here.
The atom bound is a statement about the dip, and we have not established whether the excess-mass or criticalbandwidth statistics have an analogous lattice pathology.
A bandwidth-based procedure may be protected by construction, its kernel bandwidth typically exceeding the lattice spacing, but we have not shown this and do not rely on it.
Whether the conclusions of this paper extend to those procedures is open.
